reason: The sources provide robust, multi-site verification for the Orionids' origin as debris from Halley's Comet, their orbital mechanics, and observational history.
story: Every October, skywatchers gaze up at the Orionid meteor shower, watching bright shooting stars streak across the sky near the constellation Orion. But these streaks are not falling stars at all. They are tiny crumbs shed by humanity's most celebrated cosmic traveler: Halley's Comet. As Halley swings around the Sun on its roughly seventy-six-year retrograde orbit, solar heat vaporizes its dirty ice, scattering streams of grit and pebble-sized dust along its path. Twice each year, Earth plows directly through this cosmic debris trail, igniting the May Eta Aquariids and the October Orionids. Entering the atmosphere at a blistering sixty-six kilometers per second, these ancient particles burn up into brilliant fireballs and persistent glowing trains. Even though Halley's dark nucleus has not visited the inner Solar System since 1986 and will not return until 2061, bits of its frozen crust burn above our heads every single autumn.
angle: You do not have to wait until 2061 to catch Halley's Comet: every October, Earth smashes directly into its shed crust at 66 kilometers per second, turning comet debris into shooting stars.

claims.claim: The Orionid meteor shower is created from dust and debris shed by Halley's Comet.
The Orionid shower occurs annually and reaches its peak in late October.
The apparent radiant of the Orionid meteor shower lies in the constellation Orion near Betelgeuse.
Halley's Comet is also responsible for producing the Eta Aquariid meteor shower in May.
Halley's Comet completes an orbit around the Sun approximately once every 75 to 76 years.
Halley's Comet last passed through the inner Solar System in 1986.
Halley's Comet is predicted to make its next appearance in the inner Solar System in 2061.
Orionid meteors enter Earth's upper atmosphere at a velocity of about 66 kilometers per second (41 miles per second).
Fast Orionid meteors can produce prolonged glowing trains of incandescent debris that linger for seconds to minutes.
The comet was named for Edmond Halley, who determined in 1705 that earlier sightings represented returns of the same periodic body.
The nucleus of Halley's Comet is roughly 15 to 16 kilometers long and 8 kilometers wide.
Halley's nucleus is pitch black with an albedo of around 0.03 to 0.04, reflecting only 3 to 4 percent of incident sunlight.
The European Space Agency's Giotto probe performed a close flyby of Halley's Comet in March 1986.
Spacecraft flybys determined that only about 10 percent of Halley's surface is active in expelling gas and dust jets.
Halley's Comet travels along a retrograde orbit, circulating the Sun in the opposite direction of the planets.
Halley's 1066 passage was stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry during the Norman Conquest of England.
Written historical observations of Halley's Comet extend back to at least 240 BCE in Chinese records.
In 2003, the Very Large Telescope in Chile recorded an image of Halley's Comet over 4 billion kilometers from the Sun.

disputed: Origin of the Eta Aquariids: while most sources treat them as directly spawned by Halley's debris stream, S7 notes that 1986 observations led some astronomers to suggest the shower might merely be perturbed by the comet rather than originating from it. A script should state they are traditionally linked to Halley.

Pope Callixtus III excommunicating the comet in 1456: S2 identifies this as an 18th-century invention by an anti-church writer rather than an official historical decree. A script should omit this myth.
Genghis Khan invading Europe due to Halley's 1222 apparition: S2 treats this as legend, so a script should attribute it as folklore or leave it out.

Nucleus density measurements: S4 cites a fluffy texture with a density of 0.3 g/cm3, whereas S2 and S7 cite roughly 0.55 to 0.6 g/cm3. A script should describe the nucleus generally as a low-density rubble pile.
